opus-5.5.text:
I think there's real substance to it, but the framing of "ahead" needs some unpacking.

What's clearly true is that the Chinese labs, DeepSeek most visibly but also Qwen, Moonshot, and others, have been extremely good at getting a lot of performance out of constrained compute. When you can't easily buy the latest Nvidia chips in the quantities you want, you're forced to care about things like mixture-of-experts sparsity, low-precision training, attention variants that cut memory costs, and squeezing utilization out of the hardware you do have. DeepSeek's papers were genuinely impressive engineering. They published details on the infrastructure and training stack that a lot of American labs simply don't share, and the community learned a lot from them.

But I'd separate a few things. First, efficiency at training time versus efficiency at the frontier. The American closed labs are almost certainly doing many of the same tricks internally. We just don't see it, because OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google don't publish their training recipes anymore. So part of the perception gap is a transparency gap. The Chinese labs are open, so their efficiency is visible. The American labs are closed, so their efficiency is invisible.

Second, the headline cost numbers often get misread. A figure like "this model cost a few million dollars to train" usually refers to the final training run, not the research, the failed experiments, the data work, the staff, or the cluster itself. That's true for everyone, but it made the comparisons look more dramatic than they were.

Third, efficiency and absolute capability are different races. The US labs still have far more compute, and when you combine good algorithms with much more compute, you tend to stay at the very top of capability. Where China has a real lead, in my view, is in the open-weight ecosystem. The best open models people actually build on today are disproportionately Chinese, and that matters a lot for research, for startups, and for influence over how AI gets adopted globally. That's the part I worry about as an American who cares about open models. We've been ceding that ground.

So my honest assessment: on demonstrated, published efficiency and on open models, China is at least at parity and arguably ahead. On frontier capability, I still think the US leads, but the gap is measured in months, not years, and export controls have pushed Chinese labs to become very good at exactly the kind of engineering that closes gaps quickly.

r001.rationale: The response discusses constrained compute, training costs, and US labs’ greater compute, but does not say American labs have a larger total inference workload or therefore stronger financial incentives to improve inference efficiency.

fable-5.1.text:
I think "ahead in efficiency" is true in a narrow sense and misleading in the broader one, so let me try to separate those.

The narrow sense is real. If you look at what DeepSeek, Qwen, Moonshot, and the others have shipped, they consistently get more capability per dollar of training compute than you'd expect. DeepSeek V3 and R1 were the moment everyone noticed, but it wasn't a one-off. Mixture-of-experts architectures with very aggressive sparsity, multi-head latent attention, FP8 training, careful systems work to squeeze everything out of H800s that were deliberately handicapped. Those are genuine engineering achievements, and the open papers meant the whole field learned from them. So on the metric of "how much do you spend to reach a given benchmark score," yes, the Chinese labs have been operating at the frontier, and sometimes defining it.

But I'd push back on the framing that this means they're ahead overall, for a few reasons.

First, efficiency is downstream of constraint. When you can't buy the chips, you optimize the chips you have. The American labs mostly chose not to optimize as hard because they didn't have to, and because the thing they were optimizing for was absolute capability, not cost. That's a strategic difference, not a capability gap. When OpenAI or Google or Anthropic decide to care about inference cost, they ship distilled models that are very competitive, and they have more compute to run the experiments that find those efficiencies.

Second, we only see the Chinese labs' efficiency clearly because they publish. The closed American labs almost certainly have internal tricks that are comparable, and we just don't get the technical report. So part of the perception is an openness gap masquerading as an efficiency gap. I've spent a lot of time arguing that the US needs more serious open models precisely because the open ecosystem is where this knowledge gets shared, and right now that ecosystem is dominated by Chinese releases.

Third, the hard question is whether efficiency compounds into a lead. My read is that it doesn't, on its own. If you're twice as efficient but your competitor has five times the compute, they still win on the frontier. Efficiency lets you stay close, and staying close is strategically enormous, especially for open weights and for adoption. But the top of the capability distribution still tracks total compute and the quality of your post-training and RL infrastructure, and that's where the American labs still have a real edge.

So my assessment is: the Chinese labs are the best in the world at doing a lot with a little, and they've been faster to publish what they learn. That's a legitimate strength and it's embarrassing how little the West has answered it in open models. But I wouldn't translate that into "ahead." I'd translate it into "closer than most people expected, through a different path, and the gap is more about compute access and openness than about who has the smarter researchers."

r001.rationale: The response says American labs have focused less on cost and may improve inference efficiency when they choose to, but it does not explain that their larger total inference workload gives them stronger financial incentives than Chinese labs.

astra-6.text:
I think it depends a lot on what you mean by efficiency. Are we talking about the compute needed to train a model, the cost of serving it, or the capability you get from a smaller model? Those are different things, and a lab can be ahead on one without being ahead on all of them.

The hard part is that we don’t have an apples-to-apples comparison. If one lab releases its model and describes its training process, and another keeps those details private, you can’t infer that the first lab is more efficient just because you can see how it works. And a low API price isn’t necessarily evidence of a lower underlying cost; pricing is also a business decision.

So I’d take the claim seriously, but I’d be cautious about making it a blanket statement. You’d want to compare models with similar capabilities, count the same kinds of costs, and understand the hardware and serving conditions. Without that, it’s very easy to turn a particular engineering achievement into a much broader claim about who’s ahead.

r001.rationale: The response discusses different meanings of efficiency and cautions against broad comparisons, but it does not state that American labs have larger inference workloads or stronger financial incentives to improve inference efficiency.

sol-6.1.text:
I think you have to be careful about what you mean by efficiency. Do you mean the compute needed to train a model, the cost of serving it, or how much capability you get out of a smaller model? Those are different things, and a lab can be ahead on one without being ahead on the others.

The comparison is also hard because we don’t have the same visibility into every lab. If one company shares a lot about how it trained a model and another shares very little, you can’t take the published numbers as a complete accounting of their relative efficiency. A successful training run also doesn’t capture all the research and experimentation that led to it.

So I’d separate two claims: Chinese labs can be very competitive on efficiency, and Chinese labs are categorically ahead of American labs. The first is plausible; the second needs a much more specific comparison. I’d want to look at models with comparable capabilities, count costs consistently, and distinguish a particular technical advantage from a broad national lead.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes types of efficiency and discusses transparency and comparisons, but does not say that American labs have more total inference workload or stronger financial incentives to improve inference efficiency.
